KEY POINTS

TALKING POINTS

Ask the question on the slide and let people recognise it. Then tell the story plainly and keep everyone anonymous; this is not about a person or a product.

My team runs our lab environments, and depending on the lab, some of them are treated as production. We use a corporate monitoring solution, and it is also used in lab environments we do not control: they are part of the lab, but other teams manage them. The result is a flood of alerts for solutions we do not manage.

Read the first callout. In a team meeting, someone proposed that we think about another monitoring solution, just for our lab environments. That is a reasonable reaction to alert noise. Read the second callout. The thinking stayed on-premises: our labs spread across two datacenters, so the plan started there. But our labs already extend into Azure and AWS, and a plan that starts in the datacenter leaves those parts for later. Read the third callout: the real pain was alerts for things we do not own, and a second tool does not fix ownership; it adds a second place to be flooded.

My pushback was not about the tool. I said we need more than monitoring. We need to view this as observability, start from the whole service rather than one site, and bring the labs that run in Azure and AWS into one single pane of glass from day one.

Transition: here is what I asked the team to consider.

PURPOSE

Make the second commitment measurable: an order must complete within 45 seconds with both workers answering. M07.speakerNotes:
KEY POINTS

• AWS fulfillment is required: its failure fails the order.
• Customer → Azure Front Door WAF → health-probed Azure Container Apps or AWS EKS/ALB portal.
• Either portal serves pages; footer identifies origin; both call Azure Functions coordinator.
• Coordinator accepts order, assigns one correlation ID, queues work on Azure Service Bus.
• Validation: cas26-lnx01, SCVMM-managed Hyper-V; fulfillment: EC2 in AWS.
• Both pull via outbound AMQP/TLS 5671; no inbound publishing or AWS–datacenter VPN.
• Both results are required for one order; the monitoring behind this picture is built in section 2.
• → Next: the same chain as a list of dependencies, each one required.

TALKING POINTS

Click through the order walk: the badge IIC-000042 moves from the customer to Front Door, to a portal, to the coordinator, to Service Bus, to the on-premises worker, to the AWS worker, and back to the coordinator, where it completes.

Read left to right, following a customer. The customer reaches Azure Front Door with its WAF policy. Front Door health-probes two portal origins and routes to either one: the Azure copy on Container Apps, or the AWS copy on the EKS cluster behind an Application Load Balancer. Either origin can serve the page, and the portal footer says which one did.

Both portals call the same Azure Functions coordinator. The coordinator accepts the order, assigns one correlation ID and puts the work on Azure Service Bus.

Now the two workers. The validation worker runs on cas26-lnx01, a Linux VM on the SCVMM-managed Hyper-V cluster in the on-premises private cloud. The fulfillment worker runs on EC2 in AWS. Both pull from Service Bus over outbound AMQP/TLS 5671. Nothing is published inbound, and there is no VPN between AWS and the datacenter. Each returns a result, and the coordinator completes the order only when both answer.

That is the key point: AWS is inside the order path. If fulfillment fails, the order fails, however green Azure and on-premises look.

The monitoring that watches all of this is deliberately not on this slide: section 2 builds it route by route, starting with Arc. Transition: next, the same chain written as dependencies, with every one of them marked required.

PURPOSE

Show the IIC architecture across its three boundaries and establish that the dependencies are truthful: AWS is inside the order path, not a side panel.

The order completes only when both workers answer, so AWS is inside the order path. The monitoring behind the application is covered in section 2, one evidence route at a time.

• IIC-000042 is display-only; the coordinator-assigned CorrelationId GUID joins every order row.

TALKING POINTS

Introduce the order: IIC-000042, following the 42 theme. The order number is for display. The join key is the CorrelationId, a GUID the coordinator assigns and every row of the order carries.

Read the timeline left to right. First the portal: the customer placed the order through either origin, Azure or AWS, and the coordinator records which one on its Accepted row. Second, the coordinator writes Accepted in Azure. Third, the on-premises validation worker writes its row, cloud OnPrem, component OnPremWorker; the slide calls this step OnPrem - Completed. Fourth, the AWS fulfillment worker writes its row, cloud AWS, component AwsWorker; the slide calls it AWS - Completed. Fifth, the coordinator writes Completed with Success true. That row, and only that row, means the order is complete. Any row with Success false fails the order.

Point to the fields on each record: cloud, component, stage, result and duration. With those, one query filtered on the CorrelationId shows exactly which cloud was slow or failed. A long duration on the AWS row points at fulfillment; a failed OnPrem row points at validation.

Transition: before reading orders, prove the routes that carry them.

PURPOSE

M16.attendeeNotes:
In IIC Hybrid Orders, every stage of an order writes one record to the Cas26Service_CL table with the same CorrelationId, a GUID assigned by the coordinator. The customer-visible order number, such as IIC-000042, is for display only. An order's timeline reads: the portal origin that served the customer, the coordinator accepting the order, the on-premises worker validating it, the AWS worker fulfilling it, and the coordinator completing it.

Each record carries the cloud, component, stage, success flag and duration, so a single query filtered on the correlation ID shows which environment was slow or failed. The order is complete only when the coordinator writes a successful Completed record, and any failed stage fails the order.

TALKING POINTS

Step one: place one demo-tagged order through the Front Door endpoint with Invoke-Cas26Request.ps1 and the DemoTag switch. The tag matters: faults later apply only to tagged orders.

Step two: record its correlation ID and the time. Read out the order number, the correlation ID and which origin served the portal, Azure or AWS.

Step three: read its stage records. Query Cas26Service_CL by that correlation ID and walk the rows: coordinator Accepted, on-premises worker, AWS worker, coordinator Completed with Success true.

Step four: confirm the workbook shows it. Open CAS26 service operations and find the same order, with the same timestamps.

Read the evidence box. The order completed inside the target, every stage is present, and the workbook is fresh. If any stage is missing, stop and say so; a baseline with a gap is not a baseline.

Read the footer: call something a cause only when the test and the evidence support it. A failed AWS stage next to a CPU spike on the same machine is two observations. It becomes a cause when a test, such as a repeat order or a controlled change, connects them.

One distinction separates observability from monitoring here: did the worker fail, or did we lose sight of it? A Failed stage record while the heartbeats stay fresh points at the worker. A missing record is not proof of anything yet: check whether the work was dispatched and whether it is still waiting in the queue before you call it lost visibility. M34.speakerNotes:
KEY POINTS

• Useful alerts carry meaningful conditions and context to an accountable owner.
• Condition: commitment or signal state change, not every worker CPU spike.
• Context: service · component · evidence · freshness · starting correlation ID.
• No owner means it is not our alert: the owner box is the answer to alerts for things we do not own.
• Owner: named team · permission to act · runbook; fulfillment owner or service owner.
• Outcome: service works again, proven by evidence; the alert is not recovery.
• Say: configured rules do not prove delivery; test Azure Monitor action groups end to end.
• Before: a flood of alerts, many for systems other teams own, plus three separate rules (stage failures · queue depth · latency) for one AWS fault.
• After: one entity alert on the order commitment with a named owner; fires once per state change, resolves itself; noise for someone else's system never reaches you.
• Retire old rules once the entity alert has proven itself; run both first.
• → Next: recovery is a new observation.

TALKING POINTS

Read the chain left to right. First, the condition. It should be meaningful: a commitment or a signal changing state, such as Customers can complete an order becoming Unhealthy. Not every CPU spike on every worker.

Second, context. The alert has to carry what the responder needs: the service, the component, the evidence, its freshness and a correlation ID to start from. An alert that only says a threshold was crossed sends the responder back to the beginning.

Third, the owner. A named team, with the permission to act and a runbook that says what to do. For the AWS worker that might be the fulfillment owner; for the commitment it is the service owner.

Fourth, a verified outcome. The alert is not the outcome. The outcome is a service that works again, proven by evidence.

Now the footer. A configured rule is not proof a notification was delivered. Test the action group end to end, and check that the right person actually received it. Health model alerts use the same action groups as other Azure Monitor alerts, so the same test applies.

Now make alert fatigue concrete instead of just naming it. Look back at the controlled fault: the AWS worker fails and the order fails, while heartbeats stay fresh. Without a health model, that one root cause could still trigger several separate alerts, one on the stage-failure query, one on Service Bus queue depth climbing, one on order latency, each firing on its own with no shared context, which is exactly the alert-fatigue pattern SCOM veterans remember. With the health model, you configure one alert on the entity Customers can complete an order instead. It fires once when that state changes, even though several signals are bad, uses the same action group, and resolves itself when the entity is healthy again. Same fault, same action group, one alert instead of three. Keep in mind that the old resource alert rules keep firing until you disable them.

One practical warning: do not switch off the old rules on day one. Run both for a while, compare what each catches, then retire each old rule once the entity alert has proven itself.

When moving to health model alerts, run the old rules and the new entity alert side by side, then retire each old rule once the entity alert has proven itself. The owner is also the answer to alert noise from systems other teams manage: an alert that carries an owner goes to the team that can act, and an alert with no owner is not yours. TALKING POINTS

Read the banner first. This is a working definition, not a vendor definition, and it is deliberately practical.

Walk the left column: monitoring. It collects and presents signals. It builds views, sets thresholds and raises alerts. All of that is necessary. Without measurements there is nothing to explain.

Walk the right column: observability. It explains and operates. It knows the service boundary, the dependencies between components, the impact on customers, the owner of each part, a bounded action that is safe to take, and a verified recovery. That last item matters. The job is not finished when a command succeeds; it is finished when the service is shown to work again.

Now read the join in the middle: signals plus context. Observability is not a different pile of data. It is the same measurements with the context that lets someone answer why and what next: which service, which dependency, which customer operation, which owner.

M09.attendeeNotes:
Monitoring and observability are often used as synonyms. In this session they mean different things. Monitoring collects and presents signals: it builds views, applies thresholds and raises alerts. Observability uses those signals to explain and operate a service: it knows the service boundary, the dependencies, the impact on customers, the owner, a bounded action and a verified recovery.

The link between them is context. The same measurements become explanatory when they carry enough information to say which service, which dependency and which customer operation they describe. Monitoring is a prerequisite, not a lesser form. Observability depends on good measurements and adds what is needed to reach a decision and prove its result.
